title: The Divine Economy and the Suffering of the Just
english: contrary to his courage

What is, is the absolute good to exist. For it is blessed to be outside of this life. To those who know, Jesus says: 'You are no longer of this world, but I have chosen you' (John 15:19). Therefore, it is better not to have even begun the path of such a way, even if it happens through divine economy. For it is good if no one in health needs a physician. Thus, not being in the same state follows, which also follows as something laborious and unpleasant, as it brings about: 'For he would have removed toil from my eyes' (Job 5:7). This indicates not only the one suffering and the toil surrounding him, but also that he saw many being led astray; for the eye of the righteous is weighed down by works being performed by the wicked. And the toil that encroaches upon life is not small. In injustice, all these things exist... [text garbled/unclear]... which would not happen if evil were not being done.

But even Habakkuk allows such a voice, saying: 'Why have you shown me troubles and pains, to make me see violence and unrighteousness?' (Habakkuk 1:2-3). 'Why did I not end in the womb, come out from the stomach and not immediately perish? Why did my knees meet, why did I suck breasts?' He avoids the economy intended for the benefit of others, as it seems, according to Jonah, to demand the teaching of God's judgments, which is a private matter of the righteous, not being completely ignorant, but so that others may learn this kind of speech being personified. For Jeremiah approaches thus: 'You are righteous, Lord, but I will speak judgments to you' (Jeremiah 12:1), which is indicative of knowing what happens through these, concerning which he asks: 'Why does the way of the ungodly prosper?' (Jeremiah 12:1).

The judgment of God in reality receives much variety: the unrighteous being prospered, and the righteous being distressed and partaking of filth, as Jeremiah himself, being holy and having been sanctified from the womb, suffered so many things as to be cast into a pit of mire. But also Lazarus and the rich man—the one suffering evil, the other living with much ease—bring forth the precision of God's secret judgments (Luke 16:19-31). And this 'prospering' is called so as toward the glory of the many. Therefore, the saint is not vain-speaking, but asks so that it brings about the others learning such things. This also exists in what is said in one of the Psalms: 'How good to the...'

title: The Spiritual Warfare and the Choice of Company
english: God is with the upright in heart. As for me, my feet were shaken a little, and my steps were poured out a little, because I sought peace among the lawless, seeing sinners (Job 13:15). For it does not waver, it is clear; for he says, 'How good God is to Israel' (Job 10:18). He thinks these things as being understood by those having a straight heart.

He posits himself as being shaken while being firm, and receiving the countenance of those being displeased, so that after the words of doubt, the words of teaching might be brought forward. And Job, indeed, inquiring of God, wants to learn—for this he brings forward the countenance—the cause of such a struggle. For indeed, regarding the cause of the way in the body, he says as if receiving it: for indeed... having fallen into so much evil, as if they had come to entreat for the fellowship of the body and the helpers of the providential economy, so as to say the things set forth.

'Why then did I not finish in the womb?' (Job 10:12). For the saints, in reverence, entreat that they not grasp the benefit of the weaker ones. Because of this, he also says the following: 'And from the stomach I came out and was not immediately lost' (Job 10:18); likewise also: 'Why did my knees meet [me]? Why did I suck breasts?' (Job 10:9). For the holy one willed that disease should not happen to the rational ones, so that a sequence might not occur for the pure to come through them in a medicinal manner.

And also good is: 'Why did my knees meet [me]?', which indicates a journey. For with others, because of their own faults, life followed here, but with the saints, they met not as those responsible, but as those executing an economy. 'Now, having slept, I have rested, but having awoken, I have not ceased with kings and counselors of the earth' (Job 3:13, 29:25).

For if, he says, such a sequence and order had not occurred as that which led me to this state through those needing treatment—that is, if I had happened to finish in the womb, not coming out from the stomach and being immediately cut off, and not having met knees nor sucked breasts—it would be, if not through the providential economy administered through us, 'now having slept, I have rested', which is: having ceased my course in that life of the divine and heavenly rational ones. The kings and counselors tyrannize the earth of the gentle, concerning whom it has been said: 'Blessed are the gentle, for...'

"They shall inherit the earth" (Psalm 37:11), taking for ourselves kings in high positions and counselors of a lower rank, over whom the kings rule. Such an analogy is contained in the parable in the Gospels: "become more than ten cities or five." "who were proud upon swords." The saint, not being a lover of war, did not want to have his social intercourse with such kings readily available, who, being ready to fight, consider such social intercourses to be good; but knowing "that our struggle is not against blood and flesh" (Ephesians 6:12) according to the apostle, "but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this [world], against the spiritual forces of wickedness," against whom those living well fight, having armed themselves with the salvation "panoply," he wanted to have his social intercourse without being provoked by human generation. But one of those peaceful ones was the one seen by Jesus, son of Nun, as a commander of the Lord, to whom he said: "Are you of ours or of the adversaries?".

Being discerning, the saint knows and does not readily recognize that even the adversary often "is transformed into an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). These, however, are also men, not preferring arrogance, but rejoicing in the victory over the adversaries and "rejoicing in God" (2 Corinthians 6:10). "Or with rulers, of whom there is much gold, who filled their houses with silver" (1 Timothy 6:17). Having the same mind and what has now been set forth, let us receive it familiarly with the person of the saint. For not being a lover of silver or a flatterer, it did not seem right for him to spend time with the rich, he who bravely brought about the loss of all possessions and wealth and did not accept riches, being without following friends and having a free intention and an unshakable word; how would he want to have his social intercourse with such rulers and kings, who happened to be adorned with wealth? To some, appearing as a good wealth, the wonderful Paul writes: "You have already become rich; you have reigned without us; and would that you had reigned, so that we might also reign with you" (2 Corinthians 6:10). For they have possessed much gold, which indicates a pure mind, pure ones, approaching clearly with the light of knowledge. These themselves also, by the analogy of nature, not by the spoken [word]...

title: The Meaning of Eternity and the Eternal Servant
english: By the word, they filled their own houses, having their own minds adorned by participation in the word of surpassing purity, not possessing any such state which has become Job's for the sake of the divine economy; for because of conversation and interaction with men, such a mind does not have its likeness unblemished, which would have been wiped away if it were not for sin, but because something else had happened, which occurred for the sake of the benefit of others. 'Either as a fetus proceeding from a mother's womb, or as infants, who did not see light.'

To the words 'and I suckled breasts,' this is given through the middle of the verses spoken from 'now having slept I am at rest' until 'who filled their houses with silver.' Let the same thought be applied to the previously spoken things; for just as it happened to come into existence involuntarily, so it happened for him to be in the state of a fetus, so that he might not participate in more of this kind of distraction and friction according to generation, or even if he had become an infant, to turn back again, so that he might not be born in the state of age after the infantile state.

For in truth, such a thing would not be outside of perplexity and seeking, regarding those not reaching unto life, and those dying immediately after birth, which the philosopher will investigate not as if these things happen by chance, but as being the just and good of God, the God of all things, governing all things by word and order and measure and weight. The saint himself knows the judgment and does not say this without anxiety, but praises the better state and being persuaded that this is to be preferred. 'There the impious burned a fire of wrath, there the wicked rested from the body, but the eternal ones were of one mind.'

The whole verse of the divine thought being tested by Job is a teaching upon the difference of human generation. For having understood regarding it being better for him not to approach the human way or to be born, or having been born to be immediately freed from this, he proceeds and teaches a certain cause, as if this thing was being studied not a little by the opposing powers. Since the word showed how the souls encountered various errors of generation, and the devil and those with him are lovers of sin...

Just as it stirs those given to it into wickedness, this very thing interprets by saying, 'There the ungodly burned up a fury of wrath' (Ps 58:6). By saying 'there,' he refers to the other world from this one, as in: 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, naked I will depart there' (Job 1:21).

However, even if such a thing is a mere paper against evil powers, God forewarns through His economy and has given laws to each to prevent sinning, so that while passing through this [life], one might think heavenly things and desire a similar life there, so that having worn out the body, one might have a rest as one who has become a combatant against the habit of wickedness. For this is what is meant by: 'There the combatants rested from the body' (Job 42:6).

For the saints, having been pleased, through many tribulations on earth—of which they become combatants in body and not in mind—have a rest with the angels, having attained it eternally. And if those are eternal, and their rest is communal, it is evident that the souls too are eternal; for they are immortal and, having despised the temporal, possess the eternal.

It should be noted that 'eternal' is spoken of in several ways; it also signifies the without-beginning and the without-end, as in: 'God is eternal.' For God is called eternal because His existence has neither beginning nor end. And something else is eternal, as it is said: 'The things not seen are eternal' (1 Cor 15:51). For these are not eternal as God is, but because they remain always without falling away. And differently is the eternal, when it is measured against the present, as it is said: 'The sons of this age are wiser in their own generation' (1 Cor 3:19). And the time extending the life of a man is also called an age.

Regarding the Hebrew who was unwilling to be set free in the seventh year, it is said: 'He shall be a servant for an age' (Ex 21:6). For no human being remains a servant at all through death. According to this, Paul also writes: 'If meat makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat for an age' (Rom 14:21), instead of 'through life.' 'They did not hear the voice of a tax-collector.' For this age is filled with tribute, in which one has come here for the sake of the economy. For there are many who, having come under the yoke of sin, [pay] taxes and dues to the adversary...
